title: KV cache transparent compaction scheduler notes
content:
Goal:
Design notes for a transparent compaction scheduler that runs alongside the KV cache allocator. The scheduler should reclaim fragmentation with minimal impact to tail latency and predictable CPU/GPU memory pressure. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: sketches, heuristics, and lightweight configs that we can prototype quickly in the runtime agent.

Why this is needed (short):
- Long-running replicas show progressive fragmentation in slab and slabless modes.
- Large cold KV entries cause holes that reduce effective capacity by up to 12-18% in internal sims.
- Manual compaction is disruptive; we need an automated scheduler that performs small, targeted compacts and adapts to load.

Key ideas / constraints:
- Transparent to API callers: compaction is background work, never synchronous with request critical path.
- Slice work into bounded-duration units (compaction quanta) to avoid long GC pauses.
- Prioritize compaction candidates by occupancy delta / reclaimable_bytes per work unit.
- Integrate with existing eviction policies (LRU/hybrid) so compaction avoids duplicating effort.
- Respect latency SLOs: when 95th/99th token latency exceeds threshold, scheduler backs off aggressively.
- Support two modes: conservative (low-load steady-state reclaim) and aggressive (scheduled maintenance windows or offline drains).

Data structures and signals used:
- occupancy_map (sharded per arena): estimated live_bytes / reserved_bytes per slice. (approx sketch, maintained incrementally)
- hole_index samples: bloom-ish per-shard sample of freed spans to estimate fragmentation hot spots
- recency_score histogram: combines last_accessed timestamp + request frequency over rolling N seconds
- reclaimability_score = reclaimable_bytes * (1 + fragmentation_factor) / (1 + recent_access_penalty)

Compaction candidate selection algorithm (sketch):
1) Periodic sampler wakes every T_sample ms (configurable, default 1000ms).
2) For each arena/shard gather top-K slices by reclaimability_score. K tuned by arena size.
3) For each candidate produce a compaction plan: which spans to move, expected temp buffer (scratch) and estimated CPU cycles.
4) Accept candidate if plan.cpu_est <= budget_cpu_per_tick AND estimated_io <= budget_io_per_tick AND current_tail_latency < tail_threshold.
5) Execute compaction quanta: move at most M entries or N bytes (config knob) then yield.

Memory accounting and scratch usage:
- Compaction needs a scratch buffer to materialize relocated entries. Aim for amortized scratch <= 2% of arena.
- When compaction risk would exceed scratch budget, mark candidate as deferred and increase its score slightly to avoid starvation.
- For GPU-backed caches, compaction should prefer CPU-side staging with batched device memcpy; avoid in-place GPU relocates unless we have a device-assisted copy primitive.

Eviction interplay and ordering:
- Eviction remains the first-line defense for capacity. Compaction should not trigger evictions; instead it increases usable free space so evictions are less frequent.
- When eviction pressure is high (free < low_watermark), scheduler switches to emergency mode: prioritize quick reclaim of small-but-highly-reclaimable slices, and while in emergency, reduce per-quanta cost (smaller quanta) to minimize latency impact.
- Use a lease mechanism: compaction marks affected keys as 'moving' for a short TTL so live request routing can consult the moving-table. This avoids races on concurrent reads/writes.

Metrics to track (first-pass):
- reclaimed_bytes_total (counter), reclaimed_bytes_per_minute (rate)
- compaction_runs_total and sustained_runs_active
- average_compaction_quanta_duration_ms
- compaction_scratch_utilization_pct
- fragmentation_estimate_pct (before/after compaction windows)
- tail_latency_95/99 while compaction_active (tagged)
- compaction_aborts_due_to_slo (counter)

Simulation results (local sim, synthetic workload):
- baseline occupancy 86%; after 6h of mixed workload fragmentation drifted to 73% effective occupancy.
- enabling conservative background compaction (quanta=64KB, sample 1s) restored occupancy to 83% in ~45 minutes, with 95th latency uplift +3% and p99 +7% (we consider acceptable for conservative).
- aggressive compaction (quanta=512KB, maintenance window) restored to 88% in 12 minutes, p99 spikes to 1.9x for brief windows — acceptable only for scheduled maintenance.
- memory scratch peak reached 1.9% of arena in aggressive mode, within our budget.

Operational knobs (config file keys):
- compaction.enabled = true|false
- compaction.mode = conservative | aggressive | off
- compaction.sample_interval_ms = 1000
- compaction.quanta_bytes = 65536
- compaction.quanta_time_ms = 50
- compaction.scratch_limit_pct = 2
- compaction.backoff_tail_latency_ms = 150
- compaction.max_cpu_pct = 8  # percent of core time reserved for compaction work
- compaction.priority_boost_on_defer = 1.2

Failure modes and mitigations:
- runaway compaction steals CPU -> enforce cgroups/cpu quota and kernel niceness; runtime watchdog kills compaction thread if it violates quota.
- compaction collides with hot writes -> moving-table lease with short TTL and per-key CAS ensures correctness; on collision, compaction either aborts that key or retries with exponential backoff.
- insufficient scratch buffer -> global backpressure signal to allocator; when scratch cannot be granted, scheduler delays compaction and tags slice as high-priority for later.

Compatibility notes with current allocator variants:
- slab allocator: compaction merges partially-full slabs into freeable slabs and returns freed slabs to system. Implementation touches: slab header relocation and slab-index update, incremental remapping to avoid global locks.
- slabless / pool allocator: compaction prefers coalescing adjacent free spans and re-mapping occupancy bitmaps; uses low-level copy + pointer swap under shard lock.

Tracing and observability:
- Emit a compact.plan trace event with: shard_id, candidate_id, reclaimable_bytes, quanta_bytes, scratch_requested, expected_latency_risk.
- Traces should be sampleable (default sample rate 0.01) to avoid observability costs.
- Provide a runtime endpoint to list active compaction candidates and plan debug dumps for replay in local sims.

Prototype plan & milestones (approx):
- Week 1: implement sampler + candidate scoring; no actual copy, just dry-run metrics. (Marco)
- Week 2: implement quanta executor with CPU copy path and scratch accounting. (Priya)
- Week 3: integrate moving-table and lease mechanism; tests for concurrency. (Asha)
- Week 4: GPU staging path + device memcpy experiment; observe p99 impact. (Samir)
- Week 5: dashboards and alerting; dogfood on 2x small instances.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Should compaction be tenant-aware (different priority per customer) for multi-tenant Dedicated? Likely yes, but increases complexity.
- Do we expose compaction metrics per-route? Pros: actionable; cons: high cardinality. Consider per-tenant aggregated metrics only.
- How to quantify fragmentation reliably without heavy scans? Our sampled occupancy_map approach has error bounds; need more sims across real workloads.

TODOs:
- Add a microbenchmark harness for compaction quanta (measurens: copy throughput, latency interference).
- Add end-to-end test that asserts no data loss under concurrent writes during compaction. Link: JIRA-RI-7789 assigned.
- Finalize lease semantics and TTL defaults after concurrency tests.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is deliberately implementation-opinionated; please call out any assumptions that conflict with current allocator internals.
- If we want to fold compaction into the allocator main loop rather than a separate thread, we should weigh complexity vs observability and ability to throttle independently.

Appendix: small glossary
- quanta: bounded unit of compaction work (bytes or entries)
- moving-table: transient registry of keys/spans under relocation
- scratch buffer: temporary staging region for relocated values

End of notes.
